order.words: more water, until it is like soft butter
switch it off before it is tipped out

safety.words: gloves on: wet cement burns skin
goggles on: cement dust hurts eyes
never hands or a shovel inside while it turns

little.twist: The second row has no glowing places: stagger it yourself.
little.can_now: lay a little wall with mortar, keep it level and stagger the joints
little.try_real: With a grown-up, look at a real brick wall from the pavement (never go onto a building site). Find the staggered joints, and show your grown-up how each brick sits across two below.

steps.say: Welcome to the practice building site! Today you build a little wall with big blocks, just like real builders.
Safety first! Put on the hard hat and the gloves.

lines.hard_hat: Hard hat on: it keeps your head safe.
lines.gloves: Gloves on: wet mortar is rough on skin.

steps.done: Now you are ready to build.

steps.say: Pick up the trowel and spread a bed of mortar along the line, nice and even.
steps.done: A smooth bed of mortar: the blocks will sit tight.

steps.say: Now lay the three big blocks on the mortar, end to end. Put each one where it glows.
This block sits a little high. Tap it down gently with the trowel.
Lay the spirit level along the top of the blocks and hold it still. Is the bubble in the middle?
steps.done: The bubble is in the middle: your row is level.

steps.say: Spread mortar along the top of the first row.
How should the second row start, so the wall is strong?

choices.text: With a whole block, like the first row
choices.why: Then the joints would make one straight line up the wall, and it could split there.
A gap makes it weak: blocks sit tight, with mortar between.

steps.done: Yes! A half block moves the joints along.

steps.say: Start with the half block, then the whole ones. See how each block sits across two below?
steps.done: The joints are staggered, like a jigsaw.

steps.say: Lay the second row by yourself: the half block first, and stagger the joints.
Builders test their ideas. The coach built a quick wall with its joints in one straight line. Give it a gentle push.
steps.done: It splits along the straight line of joints!

steps.say: Now give your wall the same gentle push.
steps.done: Yours stays strong: the staggered blocks lock together and share the push.

steps.say: Spread mortar on the second row.
Lay the top row: three whole blocks, each across two below.
Check the top row with the spirit level once more.
How many rows of blocks did you build?
steps.done: Three rows, one on top of another.

steps.say: Your wall is finished! Mortar, blocks, a level row and staggered joints: that is how real builders do it.

check.say: Why do builders stagger the joints?
Which tool shows that a row is level?
What do you put on first at a building site?

name_it.title: Building a wall
lines: Safety first: hard hat and gloves.
A bed of mortar, then the blocks, end to end.
Check each row with a spirit level.
Stagger the joints: each block sits across two below.
name_it.source: Brick bonds: the Brick Development Association; safe sites: the HSE

sources.fact: Bricks and blocks are laid in a bond: the joints are staggered so each one sits across two below; straight joints make a wall weak
A concrete block's face is 440 x 215 mm: one block takes the place of six bricks
Head protection and gloves on building sites; wet cement can burn skin
A spirit level's bubble sits in the middle when a surface is level

middle.twist: No glowing places on the second row, and the coach waits longer.
middle.can_now: plan a wall by measuring, lay it in bond, and say why doors need lintels and roofs slope
middle.try_real: With a grown-up, look at a brick house from the pavement. Find the lintel over a door or a window, and show your grown-up how the joints stagger round a corner.

steps.say: Welcome back to the building site! Today you build a little garden shed with real-size bricks.
Safety first! Hard hat, gloves and goggles on.

lines.gloves: Gloves on: cement is rough on skin.
lines.goggles: Goggles on: for the mixer and the saw.

steps.say: Measure the front of the shed: hook the tape on the corner peg and pull it to the other peg.
A brick and its joint take 22.5 cm. How many bricks fit along 180 cm?
Mortar is made in the mixer. In real life a grown-up runs it: you tell them the order. Press each thing in turn.
steps.done: Mortar like soft butter, mixed in the right order! Goggles off until the next dusty job.

steps.say: Pick up the trowel. Spread a bed of mortar along the front, from corner to corner.
steps.done: A smooth bed: the bricks will sit tight.

steps.say: Lay the first row: start at the corner and work along. Leave the doorway open.
steps.done: The first row, with the doorway left open.

steps.say: One brick sits a little high. Tap it down to the line with the trowel.
Lay the spirit level along the row and hold it still. Is the bubble in the middle?
Builders lay the corners first. Your team has laid the corners and the other walls. Spread mortar along your row.
Lay the second row between the corners. At the doorway it ends with a half brick, so the joints still stagger.
steps.done: Half bricks at the doorway: the bond carries on.

steps.say: Lay the second row by yourself, staggered, with half bricks at the doorway.

safe_mistake.wrong: a wall with its joints in one straight line
safe_mistake.why: A straight line of joints has nothing holding it together, so a push splits it. Staggered joints share the push.
safe_mistake.right: stagger the joints: each brick across two below

steps.say: What if the joints lined up? The coach built a test wall like that. Give it a gentle push.
steps.done: It splits along the straight joint!

steps.say: Now give your wall the same gentle push.
steps.done: Yours stays strong: the bricks lock together.

steps.say: Hold the plumb line at the top of the corner and let it hang still. Is the corner straight up?
steps.done: The string and the corner are side by side: it is plumb, straight up.

steps.label: Row by row
steps.say: Your team builds the walls up, row by row, in the same bond.

safe_mistake.wrong: bricks over an opening with no lintel
safe_mistake.why: Bricks need something under them: over an opening with no lintel they would drop in.
safe_mistake.right: a lintel resting on the wall at both sides

steps.say: The bricks over the doorway need something to sit on. What do builders put there?

choices.why: Bricks can't float: without a lintel, the bricks above would fall into the doorway.
A curtain can't carry bricks. A lintel can.

steps.done: A lintel carries the bricks and passes their weight to the wall at each side.

steps.say: Lay the lintel over the doorway, resting on the bricks at both sides.
steps.done: It rests on the wall at both ends: strong.

steps.label: To the top
steps.say: The team finishes the walls to the top.

safe_mistake.why: Sawdust and chips fly up towards your eyes. That's why goggles go on before the saw.

steps.say: Saw the rafter along the pencil line: long, slow strokes.
Up on the scaffold. Lay the three rafters from the front wall to the back.
Nail a rafter to the wall plate with the hammer: little taps first, then firm ones.
Why does a roof slope?

choices.why: A slope looks nice, but it is there for the rain.

choices.text: So birds can sit on it
choices.why: Birds like it, but the slope is for the rain.

steps.done: Yes: rain runs down the slope and off the roof.

steps.say: Lay the roof tiles row by row, from the bottom up. Each row overlaps the one below, so rain runs over the top.
steps.done: Every row overlaps the one below: the rain can't get in.

steps.say: Your shed is finished! Walls in bond, a lintel over the door, and a roof that sheds the rain.

check.say: What goes over a doorway in a brick wall?
Which tool checks that a wall is straight up?

name_it.title: Building a shed
lines: Measure first, and count the bricks.
Mortar mixed in order: water, sand, cement, water.
Rows level, corners plumb, joints staggered.
A lintel over the door carries the bricks above.
A sloping roof, its tiles overlapping from the bottom up.
name_it.source: Brickwork: the Brick Development Association; safe sites: the HSE

sources.fact: UK bricks are 215 x 102.5 x 65 mm, laid with 10 mm joints: 225 mm a brick along a row
Mortar is cement, sand and water mixed to a smooth paste
A lintel is a beam over an opening that carries the load above it
A plumb line hangs straight down, so a wall beside it can be checked for straight up
Roof tiles overlap the row below so rain runs off; pitched roofs shed water
Goggles for cutting and for cement; gloves, as wet cement can burn skin

big.twist: No glowing places on your rows, and the coach waits longer.
big.can_now: set out a square corner with 3-4-5 and explain bonds, lintels and roof tiles
big.try_real: With a grown-up, find a lintel over a real window and the half bricks at its sides. Look at a roof: which way does the rain run? Measure a real brick with a ruler: is it about 21.5 cm long?

steps.say: Welcome to the building site! Today you build a small house: walls, a door, a window and a roof.
Safety first: hard hat, gloves and goggles.
Measure the front of the house: hook the tape on the corner peg and pull it to the other peg.
A brick and its joint take 22.5 cm, and the front is about 315 cm. How many bricks long is it?
Is the corner square? The pegs are 60 cm along the front and 80 cm along the side. Measure between them.
steps.done: Exactly 1 metre: the corner is square!

steps.say: Why do 60, 80 and 100 cm make a square corner?

choices.why: Only some do: 3, 4 and 5 fit, because 9 + 16 = 25.

steps.done: Pythagoras: 3, 4, 5 always makes a right angle.

steps.say: Time for mortar. In real life a grown-up runs the mixer: tell them the order, one thing at a time.
steps.done: Mortar like soft butter. Goggles off until the next dusty job.

steps.say: You build the corner, left of the doorway. Spread a bed of mortar on the footing there.
Lay two bricks from the corner to the doorway.
steps.done: The first row of your corner.

steps.say: Lay the first row of the corner by yourself.
Check the row with the spirit level, held still.
Spread mortar on the row.
The second row: a whole brick, then a half brick at the doorway's edge, so the joints stagger.
steps.done: A half brick at the opening keeps the bond.

steps.say: The second row by yourself: staggered, with a half brick at the doorway.
Spread mortar again.
Lay the third row, like the first.
Hold the plumb line at the top of your corner and let it hang still. Is it plumb?

steps.label: Row by row
steps.say: Your team builds the walls up to the top of the window, in the same bond.

safe_mistake.wrong: bricks over an opening with no lintel
safe_mistake.why: Bricks need something under them: over an opening with no lintel they would drop in.
safe_mistake.right: a lintel resting on the wall at both sides

steps.say: What will carry the bricks over the window?

choices.text: A lintel resting on the wall each side

choices.why: Glass is not made to carry bricks. A lintel does.
Without a lintel, the bricks above would fall into the window.

steps.done: A lintel spreads the weight to the wall at both ends.

steps.say: Lay the lintel over the window.
How far does the lintel rest on the wall? Measure from the window's edge to the lintel's end.
steps.done: 21.5 cm: more than the 15 cm a lintel needs at each end.

steps.label: Up to the door's top
steps.say: The team builds up to the top of the doorway.
Now the doorway's lintel: lay it over the door.

steps.label: To the top
steps.say: The team finishes the walls.

safe_mistake.why: Sawdust and chips fly up towards your eyes. That's why goggles go on before the saw.

steps.say: Saw the rafter along its line: long, slow strokes, your other hand well away.
Up on the scaffold: lay the rafters in pairs, meeting at the top.
Nail a rafter's foot to the wall plate.
Why do roof tiles overlap?

choices.text: So rain always runs onto the tile below

choices.why: Tiles cost money: the overlap is there to keep the rain out.

choices.text: So they rattle in the wind
choices.why: The overlap keeps the rain out, and the tiles are fixed down.

steps.done: Yes: the rain runs over the top of each tile, never into the gaps.

steps.say: Lay the tiles row by row, from the bottom up, each row overlapping the one below.
Your house is finished! Walk in through your own front door.
You built it: a square corner, walls in bond, lintels over the door and the window, and a roof that sheds the rain.

check.say: Pegs 60 cm and 80 cm from a corner: for a square corner, the diagonal is...
How far must a lintel rest on the wall at each end?
What do you wear to saw wood?

name_it.title: Building a house
lines: Measure, and set out a square corner: 3, 4, 5.
Corners first; every row level, every corner plumb.
Stagger the joints, with half bricks at the openings.
Lintels rest at least 15 cm on the wall at each side.
Rafters, then tiles from the bottom up.
name_it.source: Brickwork: the Brick Development Association and the NHBC Standards; safe sites: the HSE

sources.fact: 3, 4 and 5 make a right angle (9 + 16 = 25): builders set out square corners with it
Lintels need a bearing of at least 150 mm on the wall at each end
A lintel is a beam over an opening that carries the load above it
Stretcher bond and cut bricks at openings keep the joints staggered
Tiles overlap the row below; the roof's pitch sheds rain
Eye protection for cutting; gloves for cement
